author: borntogambles
text:
Max shipped almost 40 iOS apps that make a combined $36,000 a month. He built most of them after work, around a 9-to-5.

On camera he builds a new one, a stamp identifier, in under 20 minutes.

He starts in an ASO tool, not a code editor. His logic: 75% of App Store downloads start with a search, so the keyword is the problem people pay to solve. He types "stamp identifier", filters out crowded terms, checks the competitors, and finds only 4 apps ranked above 100, all released in 2025. Young niche, weak defenders. Keyword locked.

Then the part that took years to earn: his boilerplate. Onboarding, paywall, payments, settings, all prebuilt from 40 previous apps. On top of it he sends Claude Code a 2-sentence prompt: build the camera, gallery, identification, collection and history screens, make it compile. He waits. The app runs.

His money mechanics stay identical across the portfolio. Weekly subscription with a free trial plus a yearly, and a lifetime price for single-use apps. The review prompt fires at the aha moment, right after a successful scan, and never after a failed one.

Visuals take minutes: Gemini draws the icon, competitor screenshots feed the layout, the keyword goes into the title, subtitle and a stuffed 100-character list. Submit.

His advice cuts through the whole genre: thousands of AI apps flood the store every week, so make sure your AI slop beats theirs.

An app a week, after work. The keyword does the marketing.

author: marlowxbt
text:
The most underrated desk upgrade of the year is free. It uses the iPad you already own.

A guy on GitHub released OpenSidecar. Free. Open source. peetzweg/opensidecar. You install it on a Mac and any spare Apple device becomes a full second monitor. An old iPad. An iPhone. A second MacBook.

Not a mirror. A real extension of your desktop. You drag a browser window from the Mac straight onto the iPad, scroll with your finger, move around the page like the tablet is a monitor you can hold.

Until this week, that feature cost $100. Duet Display. Luna Display. Apple's own Sidecar with a locked list of supported devices. Three paid products doing what one open source repo now does over Wi-Fi or USB with macOS 14 and iOS 17.

The real idea in the post is not the app.

The real idea is that half the people watching have an iPad in a drawer that became a YouTube player, then a coaster, then dust. It has an M1 chip and a retina display and it is sitting three feet from a laptop that would kill for the extra screen.

Do not buy a second monitor. You already have one. You forgot about it.

The demo is a live prototype. Latency under video editing and games has not been tested. But for a browser window, a Notion doc, a Slack, a spreadsheet, it just works.

The best desk upgrade of the year is not a new display. It is the device you already stopped using.

text:
AI has torched the market for junior programmers | More about Laurie, Seldo

In early 2025 I predicted that AI will create many, many more programmers, and that new programming jobs would look different. In March I checked in and found startups substituting compute for labor at record rates, with the wave of new jobs nowhere in sight. This post is the next check-in, and I have good news and bad news.

The bad news: AI has torched the market for junior programmers. The good news: the long tail of new programmers I predicted has materialized, but with a big twist: they don't call themselves programmers. Let me show you the data, and see if you believe me.

The market for young programmers has collapsed

Here's the single most important chart about AI and programming jobs, built from ADP payroll data by Stanford's Digital Economy Lab. It tracks employment of US software developers by age, indexed to October 2022:

Developers aged 22 to 25 are down 19% from their late-2022 peak. Every cohort over 30 grew over the same period, with 41-to-49-year-olds up 14%. This isn't a firm-level fluke: after controlling for shocks at the individual company level, the Stanford team still finds a 16% relative employment decline for young workers in AI-exposed jobs, and the decline concentrates specifically in occupations where AI automates work rather than augments it. Software development is just the poster child.

Other data points in the same direction. Entry-level software postings are down 28% from their 2022 peaks. Computer science graduates now have a 6.1% unemployment rate, higher than liberal arts majors, a sentence that would have gotten you laughed out of any career counseling office in 2019.

One detail worth noticing in that chart: the junior line doesn't fall off a cliff when ChatGPT launches. It peaks a couple of months before, drifts down through 2023, and then deteriorates fastest in 2024 and early 2025, which is when coding assistants stopped autocompleting lines and started completing tickets. Agentic programming is what really turned up the heat, not ChatGPT.

There are other suspects, of course. The same period saw the ZIRP unwind, the Section 174 tax change, and a post-pandemic hiring correction, and only about 4.5% of 2025's announced layoffs were actually attributed to AI by the companies doing the laying off. But the Stanford results survive controls for firm-level shocks and interest rate exposure, and none of those confounders explains why the damage is so precisely concentrated among 22-to-25-year-olds in AI-automatable occupations while their 40-year-old colleagues thrive. With ageism in tech being alive and well you would certainly have expected the opposite if the market were just tough for programmers in general.

And yet nothing else is down

Further evidence that this is specifically about programming jobs comes if you look at the wider economy, and in fact even if you look at only "computer jobs" without specifying programming specifically.

Total US employment grew 0.8% from May 2024 to May 2025. Computer and mathematical occupations grew 1.3%, faster than the economy. The count of employed software developers, per the BLS, went from 1.53 million in May 2022 to 1.69 million in May 2025, up 10% right through the AI era. Careful studies in the US, Denmark, and by Anthropic itself find no relationship between AI exposure and aggregate employment; the Danish study, using government payroll records, can rule out effects bigger than about 1%.

How can both things be true? Weight the age bands by their share of the workforce and you get your answer:

Total developer employment is up 4.4% since October 2022. Juniors (here defined by age rather than experience, a big caveat) are only about 8% of the developer workforce, so a catastrophe for them barely moves the average. Even if you double what percentage of the workforce you think they are, the aggregate stays positive. This is why every study that looks at averages finds nothing and every study that looks at juniors finds carnage. They’re looking at different parts of the same data.

The title is dying, not the work

It gets more interesting when you look at which job titles are shrinking. Same BLS data, May 2024 to May 2025:

The occupation "computer programmer," the BLS category for people who write code to someone else's specification, fell 16% in a single year. The BLS had projected that occupation to decline 6% per decade. My people, the web developers, fell 11%, and QA testers 6.5%. Meanwhile data scientists grew 12%, systems analysts 4.4%, and the broad "software developer" category grew 2%.

The jobs disappearing are the ones where the work product is code written to spec. The jobs growing are the ones where the work product is judgment about what code should exist. AI is eating a very specific kind of programming job.

The long tail showed up. It just doesn't have the job title.

Back in 2025 I wrote that AI is a new abstraction layer, and like every abstraction layer before it, it would create vastly more developers building vastly more software. I also wrote that we should call these new people "software developers," because giving them some other name would create gatekeeping where none needs to exist.

I believe I was right -- a huge new body of developers has turned up. But they don't use that title.

The software boom is real and it is measurable. GitHub added 36 million new accounts in the last Octoverse year, its fastest growth ever, more than one new developer per second, and 121 million new repositories, the biggest year for repository creation in the platform's history, and that’s shown up as their infrastructure creaking at the joints. Eighty percent of those new arrivals used Copilot within their first week. The single biggest developer influx ever recorded arrived AI-native, at exactly the moment paid junior hiring collapsed.

My favorite evidence is the App Store, because publishing an iOS app is a costly, gated act: a $99 developer fee, a review process, a working binary. It measures shipped software, not tutorials.

New App Store submissions declined for eight consecutive years after peaking in 2016. In 2025 they grew 24%, the first real growth since the peak, and in Q1 2026 iOS submissions were up 80% year over year. The surge is so large that Apple's review times have stretched from two days to weeks. And the category mix shifted toward productivity, utilities, and lifestyle apps, which is exactly what you'd expect from first-timers solving their own problems rather than studios chasing game revenue.

Who are these people? According to Vercel, 63% of vibe-coding users are non-developers. Lovable says 60% of its users are “non-developers”, and its users create over 100,000 new projects every day. Replit claims 50 million people have used its platform. These are marketers, founders, teachers, analysts, and product managers, and they are writing software, which in my book makes them developers. They just don't identify that way, and more importantly it's not their job title, and job titles are what labor statistics count.

So the long tail of new developers materialized, on schedule and at scale. But it materialized as a capability spreading through every job title instead of as headcount in one job title. A marketing manager who vibe-codes her own attribution dashboard shows up in the BLS data as a marketing manager. The market that collapsed is the market for the credential. The activity is booming.

Where does the next generation of senior devs come from?

So my 2025 prediction scores as: right about the developers, wrong about the title. Which sounds like a happy ending until you ask what happens next.

The career on-ramp for professional software engineers used to work like this: you got hired to write mediocre code, a senior engineer reviewed it, you slowly absorbed judgment through repetition and correction, and a decade later you were the senior engineer. That chain is now broken. AI now writes the mediocre code, so nobody hires the junior developer, so nobody is in the queue to become the senior who reviews things.

Meanwhile millions of new builders are shipping with no one reviewing anything. A Veracode study found 45% of AI-generated code fails basic OWASP security tests. An audit of vibe-coded apps found 10% with critical row-level security flaws exposing user data. Apple is drowning in submissions it can't review fast enough. The software is getting built. The judgment layer is not keeping up with it, and the mechanism that used to build it, apprenticeship inside employment, has collapsed.

There are a few promising green shoots in the scorched landscape for junior devs. IBM is tripling entry-level hiring on the theory that AI-equipped juniors can do formerly senior work, redesigning the junior role around customer contact and specification rather than typing. But on the other hand, Salesforce hired zero engineers last fiscal year. Those are the two candidate futures, and which one wins determines whether the profession has senior developers in 2036.

Is a turnaround already happening?

One logical outcome of a market that doesn’t hire junior developers is that we would start feeling the pain and correct ourselves. That maybe, maybe is already happening. Indeed's postings data actually bottomed in May 2025 and has risen for thirteen straight months, up 10% year over year.

If the 22-to-25 employment line turns upwards in Stanford's next update, it may be that the market has found a new equilibrium. Look for other major employers ramping up programs like IBM’s. If we don’t see them, we are going to have to create them, or this whole boom in software creation will turn to bust.

We have to rebuild the ladder

We are not watching the death of programming. We are watching programming stop being a job title and become a capability, the same way "typist" stopped being a job title when it became a thing everyone was expected to know. That transition is going fine for everyone except the people who were about to start climbing the old ladder when we set it on fire. They're the ones we owe a new ladder, and if we don’t build it for them, we will also feel the pain.

authorName: Lian Lim | Dashboard & AI Automation Expert
text:
🚨BREAKING: Apple has blocked agentic AI from the App Store for years.

this week, one finally got through.

OpenClaw just launched native iOS and Android apps.

the reason Apple approved it is in the privacy label.

WHAT JUST HAPPENED:

OpenClaw dropped native mobile apps for iOS and Android.

the launch thread pulled 1.5 million views within hours.

the App Store listing reads: "Data Not Collected."

that line is why it cleared review.

nothing routes through a company server.

your data and automations live on your own gateway.

Apple had no data practices to object to.

HOW IT WORKS:

the phone does not run the AI.

it pairs with your self-hosted OpenClaw Gateway running on a Mac, Linux box, or Windows machine.

scan a QR code. your phone becomes a node in your personal agent network.

→ chat with your agent or switch to real-time Talk mode
→ approve or deny every action the agent wants to take
→ grant optional access to camera, location, photos, contacts, calendar
→ on android: "hey google, ask OpenClaw" routes straight into the app

your agent lives on your hardware.

your phone is the remote.

THE NUMBERS:

→ 247k GitHub stars in under three months
→ 1.17 million weekly npm downloads
→ 5,400+ installable skill packs
→ 20+ connected channels: telegram, whatsapp, signal, slack, discord, imessage

THE CATCH:

→ not a standalone app. no gateway, no agent
→ setup requires a terminal. this is still an operator tool
→ early android reviews are rough. crashes and pairing issues reported
→ prompt injection warnings still apply. approvals matter

THE BIGGER PICTURE:

every AI company is racing to put an assistant in your pocket.

OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic are all shipping cloud agents.

OpenClaw just shipped the opposite.

the agent stays on your machine.

the cloud never sees your data.

and Apple, the most privacy-obsessed gatekeeper in tech, let it through the wall first.

google is reportedly building a 24/7 personal agent to compete with it directly.

it’s as if the open source project is moving faster than the trillion dollar companies.

the phone in your pocket just became a control surface for an agent you own.

not rent.

own.

text:
大学の英語の発表、お題自由だったので迷わず自分のアプリ「FesRegi」の話にしますｗ
ユーザー785人、登録模擬店262店、注文19,700件、iOSは1週間で200DL数字にすると改めてすごいなと実感
英語頑張ります💪

Hello, everyone. Today, I want to talk about something I made. It is called "FesRegi." FesRegi is a free app for school festivals. It helps students sell food and drinks easily. I made this app by myself.

In high school, I worked at a food stall at my school festival. We used paper to write orders. It was slow, and we often made mistakes. So, I thought, "I will make my own app." Now, with FesRegi, students can use a computer or a smartphone as a cash register. Customers can also order from their phone with a QR code. No more long lines!

Now, FesRegi is used in many schools. Let me show you some numbers. More than 785 people use FesRegi now. More than 260 shops are registered. And students have made about 19,700 orders with this app! I am very happy about these numbers.

There is more good news. On June 29, I released an iOS app for FesRegi. It is very new, only about one week old. But already, more than 200 people downloaded it! I think many more people will use it in the future.

In conclusion, FesRegi is a free, easy, and useful app for school festivals. It helps students sell things without stress. If your school has a festival, please try FesRegi. Thank you for listening!

私が高校生のとき、文化祭の模擬店で働いていました。私たちは紙に注文を書いていました。遅くて、よく間違えていました。それで、「自分でアプリを作ろう」と思いました。今、FesRegiを使えば、生徒はパソコンやスマートフォンをレジとして使えます。お客さんもQRコードを使って自分のスマホから注文できます。もう長い行列はありません！

 今、FesRegiは多くの学校で使われています。いくつかの数字を紹介します。現在、785人以上がFesRegiを使っています。260店舗以上が登録されています。そして、生徒たちはこのアプリで約19,700件の注文をしました！私はこの数字にとても満足しています。

 もっと良いニュースがあります。6月29日に、FesRegiのiOSアプリをリリースしました。とても新しく、まだ1週間ほどです。しかし、すでに200人以上がダウンロードしてくれました！これからもっと多くの人が使ってくれると思います。 

結論として、FesRegiは無料で、簡単で、学校の文化祭に役立つアプリです。生徒がストレスなく物を売るのを助けます。もしあなたの学校に文化祭があれば、ぜひFesRegiを試してみてください。聞いてくれてありがとうございました！

🦞 OpenClaw launches a native iOS app

OpenClaw, the open-source AI agent, now has a native app for iPhone and iPad. Until now, mobile access mainly relied on messaging apps like Telegram. The new app provides a dedicated interface for managing your AI agents on the go.

OpenClaw runs on your own Mac or PC and connects to models such as Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, and others through their APIs. The iOS app doesn't run the AI itself—it securely pairs with your self-hosted OpenClaw Gateway, letting you chat with agents, approve actions, and access device features remotely.

The app is available now as a free download on the App Store.

that experience changed a lot for me.

author: sondesix
text:
Alongside the Reno16 Series, OPPO also launched the new OPPO Bubble.

It is essentially a small display for remote camera preview/control that can be magnetically attached to the rear side of your phone.

It is useful to see your pose and composition when your phone is placed elsewhere or when someone else is taking the photo for you.

Here’s what you can do with it:
✅ Shutter button
✅ Zoom control (with pre-determined zoom levels: 0.6x, 1x, 2x, and 3.5x, it depends on the phone model)
✅ Switch between the photo and video modes
✅ Rear camera mirror and timer/countdown
✅ Switch the preview modes from full-view and fit-to-width
✅ Adjust the brightness of the badge with 3 different levels (up to 600 nits brightness)

OPPO Bubble works effectively as a remote camera control from up to 10 metres away.

During my testing period, I really love using the OPPO Bubble as I think it is truly helpful when taking a group photo or direct my friends/family to frame the photo.

The display looks gorgeous too, as it is a 1.73” OLED panel that is bright and vibrant.

That means your wallpapers will also look stunning here, as if you’re viewing it on the phone’s screen.

Unlike other similar solutions, OPPO Bubble is very thin and lightweight, at only 7 mm thick & 27.5 grams in weight. It is also IP54-certified for dust and splash resistance.

The battery capacity itself is at 560 mAh, rated to last for up to 49.7 hours when displaying a static image or 7.8 hours when continuously displaying the camera preview.

But, I found several things that I need OPPO to fix via a software update (or for the next-gen product):
• The functions are limited to camera control and adjusting a few system settings (brightness, screen lock, and scheduled screen off).
• It would’ve been so much better if the camera app functionality is expanded, for example: LED flash control, switching to more modes, EV control, filter picking, and more.
• It would’ve been awesome if they can expand the functionality, for example: music control, stopwatch/timer, notification peeking, and more.
• The magnet on the rear side of the Bubble is not as strong as I expected, so when placed on a magnetic case, it can easily move around or rotate, which makes it a bit harder to use.
• It is supposed to work with the Reno16 Series, but none of those phones have an included magnetic case or a magnetic back cover. You have to add the magnets on your own to attach it to the back side of your phone.
• Even though the circular shape might be visually appealing, it makes the viewfinder narrower and more limited.
• I found some software issues that happened quite rarely, like how it would fail to change the wallpaper, the connection suddenly dropping, and the camera app opening slowly.

OPPO Bubble is currently supported by 13 OPPO phones (Find X8/X9 Series, Reno16 Series, Reno14/15 Series except the F models), and compatibility with other devices will be coming soon.

Also, OPPO will extend support for OPPO Bubble to iPhone X and later models, running iOS 15 or later.

The full rollout is expected to be completed by July 7 in the worldwide market.

I think the potential of this device is extremely high. With a few tweaks, refinements, and better readiness, I can assure you that it will be a successful product.

• It would’ve been so much better if the camera app functionality is expanded, for example: LED flash control, switching to more modes, EV control, filter picking, and more.
• It would’ve been awesome if they can expand the functionality, for example: music control, stopwatch/timer, notification peeking, and more.
• The magnet on the rear side of the Bubble is not as strong as I expected, so when placed on a magnetic case, it can easily move around or rotate, which makes it a bit harder to use.
• It is supposed to work with the Reno16 Series, but none of those phones have an included magnetic case or a magnetic back cover. You have to add the magnets on your own to attach it to the back side of your phone.
• Even though the circular shape might be visually appealing, it makes the viewfinder narrower and more limited.
• I found some software issues that happened quite rarely, like how it would fail to change the wallpaper, the connection suddenly dropping, and the camera app opening slowly.

OPPO Bubble is currently supported by 13 OPPO phones (Find X8/X9 Series, Reno16 Series, Reno14/15 Series except the F models), and compatibility with other devices will be coming soon.

Also, OPPO will extend support for OPPO Bubble to iPhone X and later models, running iOS 15 or later.

The full rollout is expected to be completed by July 7 in the worldwide market.

I think the potential of this device is extremely high. With a few tweaks, refinements, and better readiness, I can assure you that it will be a successful product.

author: arnaudmercier
text:
Hello and welcome to Eye on AI. In today’s edition…Rabbit launches Teach mode for the R1; Microsoft and HarperCollins strike a deal for training data; Google gives Gemini memory; an AI pioneer cites OpenAI’s upcoming model when urging for regulation; Stanford ranks countries on how vibrant their AI ecosystems are. 

Rabbit, maker of the handheld orange AI-in-box device known as the R1, today released a new capability called Teach mode. The mode allows users to “teach” their devices how to perform specific actions by describing the process step-by-step on a computer using natural language and then syncing the lessons to their R1. 

The new capability is a step toward Rabbit’s vision of an app store for model actions—and ultimately, an entirely new way of interacting with devices sans the graphical user interfaces to which we’ve become accustomed. It’s also the latest release from a company that has largely been building its product in public (and Teach mode will be no exception). Critics blasted the R1 at launch as clunky, basically useless, and more of a prototype than a finished product. In conversation with founder and CEO Jesse Lyu ahead of the Teach mode announcement, he described how the company has been using the criticism and user feedback to improve the product, pushing over 20 updates including a second generation of its LAM (large action model) system that makes it possible to interact with any site rather than just the four services available at launch. He framed this back-and-forth as essential, purporting that the only way to build in the AI era is to put a product out in the world and iterate from there. 

An app store for actions

If you watch any of the demo videos for Teach mode, you may think it looks like the most tedious way possible to do something. Take one example where an early tester teaches the device how to draft a tweet. On his computer, he instructs the program to “click the icon to open the box to compose a tweet,” “click inside the text box to start typing,” “type your text inside the box,” and so on before syncing the lesson to the R1.

No coding is required, but it’s still far more involved than just drafting a post on a smartphone or laptop as we always have. Rabbit’s idea, however, is that eventually most users won’t be doing any of this tedious work or interacting with Teach mode at all. Rather than teaching the R1 actions themselves, they will be able to go into an app store of sorts and buy actions created by others. (That’s a bit ironic seeing as Rabbit talks about doing away with apps.)

The store isn’t launching with Teach mode today, however, and Lyu said there’s no timeline for it as they still need to figure out how it will be monetized (both for the company and users who create the actions)to make money from it. For now, users will have access to a limited number of lessons created by early Teach mode testers or be able to create their own. 

“You can imagine, like you train an agent, you should be able to choose whether you want to keep it public or you keep it private. And if you choose to publish it to the public community, and then if a million others are using your license, you should get paid. You should be able to benefit from it, right?” Lyu siad. “So I think this is, to us, the app store for iOS, but for agents.”

The “experimental” disclaimer

The press release announcing Teach mode states that it’s still “experimental” and that “output can be unpredictable.” This is becoming a common disclaimer with the launch of generative AI products. Anthropic, for example, said the same last month when it released Computer Use, which enables its model to use computers the way people do.

Lyu believes this is intrinsic to the nature of how AI works (models aren’t pre-programmed, so you’ll never know exactly what they’ll do) and a result of how fast the technology is developing. 

“You have to kind of encounter all the edge cases and tweak on a fly and continue. That’s just the whole nature of developing with AI models,” he said. In the case of Rabbit in particular, he also also pointed to how the startup doesn’t have a 10-year runway or the resources of a tech giant that would enable it to take its time. “We have to make sure that we take our shot and move fast. This is the only way that we can stay in competition.”

This isn’t to say Rabbit isn’t testing or taking care of issues before launch. The company collaborated with 20 testers to create more than 400 lessons, had them work with the company’s engineers in a dedicated Slack group, and implemented improvements and security safeguards prior to the Teach mode launch. Still, to many who have seen the “move fast and break things” mantra of the tech industry play out, Lyu’s philosophy may sound concerning. In AI safety and responsibility circles in particular, there’s growing conversation about how companies should be seeking out every edge case internally before launch. And as my colleague Jeremy Kahn noted in Tuesday’s newsletter, some believe it’d be a good idea to slow the whole train. 

Who’s using the R1, anyway?

As Rabbit continues to work out its kinks, who’s using it? And for what? 

Teenagers, Lyu said, are currently the driving force of the product. On the flip side, he said they have elderly users who find just pressing the button easier than navigating apps on a smartphone. Additionally, it’s finding uses in specific industries: doctors who use it for translation when speaking with patients, and truck drivers who can’t use a smartphone while driving but can hit one button on the R1, similar to how they use the radio in their truck. 

While it’s easy to still see the R1 as cumbersome and unnecessary, these examples of how it’s being used show it may have some potential. I wouldn’t count out the R1 (well, a future version of it) just yet. 

And with that, here’s more AI news. 

Sage Lazzaro

author: greggavinrfp
text:
We’re currently hard at work improving the response quality of our agentic swarm on the private edition Mac app for VeriRFP, using on-device AI while also pushing response speed. On the side I’ve been building something that came straight out of frustration at home.
My wife and daughter constantly complain about how exhausting social media has become. The endless rage bait, doomscrolling, and algorithms that seem designed to keep everyone angry and scrolling. It got me thinking there has to be a better way for adults to actually connect with people nearby.
That’s why I started MetroMeet. An 18+ social app built for real, low-pressure connections in your own area. The tagline says it best: “Meet people, not arguments.”
It’s a modern take on the fun, local, playful social apps a lot of us remember from earlier days of the internet. Your area’s wall where people post plans, questions, and everyday thoughts. Real verified profiles with personality. Simple games and icebreakers so conversations actually start. Optional private filters for compatibility — including partisanship if you want — so you can choose who sees you and who you interact with. You earn MetroBucks just by showing up and being decent, and you can spend them on virtual gifts or other playful stuff.
We launch city by city once enough locals join the waitlist. That way every area starts with real density and energy instead of a ghost town. No video feeds. No influencers. No algorithms pushing outrage. Just relationship-first connection over endless scrolling.
I just shipped the waitlist site yesterday at https://t.co/uwawqQSEig. If this resonates, claim your founding spot. Early members get priority access when their area launches, a founding badge, starting MetroBucks, and referral boosts.
We’re moving fast on the iOS side too and would love your thoughts.
What do you miss most about the earlier, lighter days of social apps, or what would actually make one enjoyable again for adults?

author: tekscreate
text:
Cursor just shipped a native iOS app — and it changes how I think about AI coding agents.

The core insight is simple: inspiration doesn't always happen at a desk. The Cursor iOS app lets you start agents, review diffs, and merge PRs from your phone. Voice input, slash commands, push notifications when agents finish.

But the architecture is what's interesting. The app connects to agents running either locally or in Cursor's cloud VMs. You can start a task locally, shift it to the cloud mid-task, and pull it back to your machine to test before merging. The mobile app is the control layer in the middle.

Real-world workflows they highlight:
- On-call incidents: get paged at lunch → launch an agent from your phone → a PR is waiting when you get back
- Customer bugs: reproduce and fix while away from your desk
- Design feedback: screenshot X/Twitter feedback → annotate → send as visual context to an agent

Cloud agents run in isolated VMs with full dev environments. They produce demos, screenshots, and logs. Push notifications and Live Activities keep you updated without staying in the app.

This is the shift: AI coding assistants are moving from desktop tools to always-on infrastructure. Agents that run in the background, report back when ready, and don't need a developer staring at a screen.

author: tekscreate
text:
Google just shipped AI Edge Eloquent — a free dictation app that removes filler words in real time, runs entirely offline, and it's already on iOS.

No internet needed. Your voice data never leaves the device.

Here's why this matters more than another transcription tool:

Most dictation apps transcribe everything — every "um", "uh", mid-sentence correction, restart. You get raw speech as text, which still needs editing. AI Edge Eloquent flips this: it captures what you MEANT to say, not what you actually said.

The offline engine uses Google's Gemma architecture on-device. Enable online mode and it taps Gemini for deeper cleanup, smart rewrites, and key-point extraction.

You can import your Gmail contacts and jargon via Dictionaries tab — names, niche terms, industry acronyms. Accuracy improves over time as it learns your vocabulary.

Output options:
- Polish → clean, readable text
- Key Points → summary (online only)
- Formal / Short / Long rewrites

Plus WPM stats and word count — useful for anyone tracking speaking clarity.

Why I'm watching this: Google is quietly building the on-device AI stack. Gemma → AI Edge → now Eloquent. The same pattern as Pixel's on-device AI features — but this time it's a standalone iOS app, not tied to any hardware.

If it comes to Android, it replaces Wispr Flow, MacWhisper, and SuperWhisper for anyone who values privacy over cloud features.

Free, no account required, works offline. That's a rare combination.

text:
Meta quietly launched Pocket — an AI app that generates playable mini-games and interactive apps from a text prompt.

The company calls these "gizmos." Describe what you want, and Pocket builds a playable interactive experience — complete with touch reactions, camera access, sound effects, and phone-movement sensing. You can publish to a discovery feed where others play or remix your gizmo.

Key details:
- Launched June 29 on iOS and Android
- Built from Gizmo technology — Meta hired the Gizmo team earlier this year and licensed their tech
- Gizmo had 635K installs with 98% positive sentiment
- Meta's Superintelligence Labs is behind it
- Still in early testing — not available everywhere yet

This is a different bet than Meta's other AI products. Meta AI generates images. Vibes generates videos. Pocket generates *interactivity* — apps and games that react to touch, movement, and the real world through your camera.

The Gizmo acquisition makes more sense now. Meta didn't just buy a team — they bought a distribution model for AI-generated software. Think of it as the TikTok of mini-apps, but instead of scrolling videos, you're scrolling playable AI-generated experiences.

The question: will the quality bar hold up when millions of users start generating gizmos? Gizmo's 98% positive sentiment on 635K installs suggests a tight feedback loop. Scaling that without quality degradation is the hard part.

Download link is live on both stores if you want to try it.

text:
Google just shipped a dictation app that runs entirely on-device — no internet required, no audio leaves your phone.

Google AI Edge Eloquent is free on iOS and does something most transcription tools don't: it strips filler words ("um," "uh") in real time and smooths your phrasing before you see the text.

The offline mode runs on Google's Gemma architecture directly on your device. Connect your Gmail to import custom names and jargon. The Dictionaries tab lets you add niche terms manually.

Online features tap Gemini for deeper cleanup, summaries, and rewrite styles (formal, short, long). But the base experience works without any network.

Why this is interesting:
- Privacy-first: voice data never leaves the device
- Real-time filler word removal — not post-processing
